title: A month of moments. One film
say: Rewind gives a small group one shared film from a month of everyday moments.
transition: First, the problem and the product boundary.
script: Good afternoon. I am Gopal Guruprasath, presenting Rewind for Team 14: a month of everyday moments from a small private group, turned into one shared film.

title: Everyday moments need a shared reason to return
say: The problem is fragmented memories in busy group chats.
The product uses small groups, a 28-day cycle and weekly contribution limits.
Photo and video both stay; the iPhone experience is the Home Screen app.
transition: The four sprints show how we delivered this boundary.
script: Our business problem is simple: people already capture moments, but the moments disappear inside busy chats and camera rolls. A group has no common point at which to look back together. Rewind adds that point. Two to ten members contribute photos or short videos, and the contributions remain sealed until a twenty-eight-day cycle closes. Each member has five moments and thirty seconds per week. The limit keeps the contribution small enough to become a habit. At the end, the group receives one film and a twenty-four-hour premiere before the film remains in Archive. Our scope is the real-account web and PWA journey: identity, private groups, invitations, capture, chat, reminders and films. That is the boundary used in the design and in the demonstration.

title: Four sprints took Rewind from foundation to hosted real accounts
say: The four milestones move from a runnable skeleton to real accounts and stabilisation.
Each of our five members has an agreed twenty-percent effort share.
Planning and reviews happened each sprint; retrospective actions changed the next sprint’s checks.
transition: The use cases now give that scope a formal boundary.
source: records/TEAM.md · AGILE.md · charts/velocity.png · open issues checked 26 Oct
script: We used four sprints with zero-based names. Sprint zero built the runnable foundation; Sprint one integrated capture, the cycle and Archive; Sprint two delivered real accounts, private S3 media, PostgreSQL and Cognito; Sprint three concentrated on stability, recovery and regression tests. Velocity, as issues closed in each sprint window, was forty-four, one hundred, one hundred and forty-five and thirty. Today the real-account web and PWA journey runs end to end on hosted dev, and three hundred and nineteen of three hundred and twenty-nine backlog issues are closed. We held project planning, and Sprint Planning and Sprint Review every sprint. Done means the outcome checked in the cheapest real environment, fast tests, a green Quality check and a merge to dev.

title: Four burndowns, velocity and each member’s share of the effort
say: Four burndowns, velocity and each member’s share of the effort
script: These are the four sprint burndowns and the velocity. Sprint one is the clean case: fifty issues in scope, thirty-seven open at the start and zero by the twenty-third of September. Sprint two is the counter-example: scope kept growing, to one hundred and thirty-five, as real accounts landed, and it closed with nine open. Velocity peaked in Sprint two with one hundred and forty-five issues closed and one hundred and thirty-two pull requests merged. Effort was not equal: I carried forty percent; Nguyen Kim Long, Jiang Jiayu and Phan Mai Tan Loi twenty percent each; Sang Haoxiang made a minimal contribution. Each retrospective changed the next sprint: integration gaps led to real adapters, stale state led to interaction tests.

title: Fourteen use cases follow one private-group journey
say: Read the human goals inside the boundary before following implementation details.
CU-B is close cycle, compile and release the group film.
transition: The logical view shows where those responsibilities live.
script: The use case view starts with user goals. Members join a private group, contribute, chat and watch; the owner also manages membership and settings. The boundary makes the secondary systems explicit: identity, object storage, web push and scheduled time. For detailed design I follow CU-B: close the cycle, compile the film and release it, which joins UC07 and UC08.

title: One Node application keeps rules close to transactions
say: We chose a modular monolith because the private-group rules share transactions.
PostgreSQL stores durable state and S3 stores media.
Interfaces isolate identity, storage and capture differences.
transition: Now map the analysis responsibilities onto that implementation.
script: The main architecture decision is a modular monolith. Splitting membership, contributions and cycles into services would add coordination without helping this workflow; keeping the rules beside one transaction makes acceptance and cycle transitions easier to reason about. Hosted PostgreSQL holds durable relational state, private S3 holds media, and Cognito supplies web identity. Adapters keep those protocols out of the domain decisions.

title: Analysis responsibilities become named implementation modules
say: The analysis model names responsibilities before implementation.
The design model maps those responsibilities to real modules and tables.
Function modules are labelled as modules, not invented classes.
transition: The hardest design problem is safely repeating this background work.
script: The left side is analysis: a boundary receives interaction, a control coordinates the use case, and entities hold the state the business must retain. On the right we refine those responsibilities into real names. The scheduler finds work, lifecycle owns the cycle transition, compilation prepares and finalises the film, and the database keeps cycles, jobs and frozen inputs. A collection of functions is drawn as a module; a class symbol is reserved for a real class, so the model stays traceable to the code.

title: Durable claims make a repeated tick safe: close, claim, render, fence
say: Follow close, claim, render and finalise in that order.
The alternatives show duplicate ticks and stale workers.
A retry reuses durable state instead of creating a second film.
transition: The same reasoning gave three more named patterns.
script: This sequence is our hardest design problem: a scheduler tick can repeat, and an old worker can finish after its lease expires. Polling alone finds work but does not make repetition safe, so we compared State and Command object hierarchies with persisted state plus a durable job, and chose the durable job. One lifecycle transaction closes the cycle, freezes the inputs, queues the film job and opens the successor. The worker claims the job and renders outside the transaction. At finalisation it proves it still holds the current lease and generation, so a repeated tick reuses the job and a stale worker cannot publish.

title: Three design problems, three named patterns in the code
say: Three design problems, three named patterns in the code
script:
Three more design problems, each solved with a named pattern; click a diagram to enlarge it. Top left, media storage: local disk in development and private S3 when hosted. MediaStore is the Strategy, with a local and a private-S3 implementation, and the S3 side adapts the AWS SDK, so the worker never branches. Top right, chat: every open screen needs each new message, so RealtimeHub is the Observer subject and each SSE connection subscribes. Bottom left, persistence: hosted PostgreSQL has a different API from local SQLite, so PostgresDatabase is an Adapter behind one data-access contract. Bottom right sums it up: problem, pattern, benefit.

[Cite if asked] Repeated work: lifecycle.ts and jobs/compilation.ts (the durable job on slide 8). Storage: privateTransport adapts the AWS SDK commands. Chat: stored messages replay on reconnect.

title: Keys preserve membership and the film’s exact input set
say: Membership is a relation used by access decisions.
Cycles own contributions and durable media jobs.
Frozen compilation inputs preserve the film’s exact input set.
transition: The cycle statechart came before the screens.
script: This is the database schema for the same use case. Membership relates an account to a group and its role, and every access decision uses it. A group has cycles; a cycle has contributions; media jobs retain processing state. Compilation inputs freeze exactly which media belongs to a film, so a retry cannot reinterpret a changing collection. We chose PostgreSQL because this path depends on joins and transactions across related records. Before the screens, one more model: the cycle’s states.

title: The cycle’s states were fixed before any screen
say: Collecting → revealing (unpublished) → published premiere → archived; the server owns every transition.
transition: Each screen then maps to one of these states.
script: Stored lifecycle state and durable jobs make work recoverable; a current lease and generation determine who may finalise.

title: Each screen renders one state of the cycle
say: Home, capture, developing, premiere and Archive each render one server state.
transition: Testing checks those states through their real boundaries.
script:
[Click inside the page to step through a flow; Esc returns to the slides. If the page does not load, press S for the storyboards.]

The screens came second, and each one maps to a state. While the cycle is collecting, Home shows the countdown, the week and the member’s allowance, and capture is offered. When the cycle closes, Home shows the film developing. Once it is published, the premiere card opens the film for twenty-four hours, and after that the film lives in Archive. Every screen reads the server’s state instead of keeping its own, so a refresh or a second device always agrees.

say: Fast suites block every merge; browser checks join for main; load and the real-account journey run on demand.
transition: Start at the bottom: static checks.

Blocks merge means the required Quality check turns red and the pull request cannot merge; reports means the result is recorded for review but never stops a merge. The top six block every pull request; browser, PWA and accessibility checks join for pull requests to main; the real-account journey and the load test run on demand. I will group them as unit, integration, end-to-end and security.

title: Six test layers, each with a real example of what it catches
say: Six test layers, each with a real example of what it catches
script: Six layers, each with a real example. Unit and component tests: one thousand six hundred and seventy-four Jest tests check screens and state without a device, with node:test for server units. Integration: one thousand and six server tests call the real routes over HTTP, and the same suite runs again on PostgreSQL 17, so a dialect difference or migration drift fails the pull request. These block every merge. End to end, forty-one Playwright tests drive the exported app with an owner, an invited member and an outsider; the PWA build is checked as it will be installed; and axe with keyboard tests checks the main screens for WCAG 2.1 AA. Those three join for pull requests to main. Each card names one real test and the bug it catches.

title: A regression test for a real bug, and security inside the suites
say: A regression test for a real bug, and security inside the suites
script:
One real bug shows why we test behaviour. After a failed photo, Try again did nothing, because retry called capture from a state whose guard returned at once. The regression test fails the capture, taps Try again and expects the viewfinder and a fresh capture: it fails on the old code and passes with the fix. Security is also tested inside the suites: cross-group privacy denials, rate limits, our patched dependencies and the scan gates themselves. The pipeline scans come in the CI/CD section, and performance in the system demo.

[Cite if asked] Regression test: camera-capture.characterisation.test.tsx. Rate limits: safety-rate-limits.test.mjs. Patched dependencies: braces and node-forge, where the original node-forge accepts a forged signature. Access tests cover account safety too; scan gates reject expired, wrong or incomplete scans.

say: Source management: work starts on an issue branch from the latest dev and enters dev only through a pull request. The dev rule requires the check named Format,
transition: Now zoom into the pull request band.
script: Source management: work starts on an issue branch from the latest dev and enters dev only through a pull request. The dev rule requires the Format, lint, typecheck, and test check, an up-to-date branch and resolved conversations, applies to administrators, and forbids force-pushes and deletion. Main adds one approving review and the browser and PWA checks. Artifact management: Git keeps source, the lockfile, workflows, Terraform and Dockerfiles. title: Nine Quality jobs feed one required merge check; security reports beside it

transition: Beside Quality, the security workflows run and report.

This is quality.yml on a pull request. The first job classifies the change; a code change fans out into eight parallel lanes: four static checks, the production dependency audit, root and IaC tests, server tests on SQLite with coverage, the same suite on PostgreSQL 17, frontend Jest with a seventy percent statement floor, and the deployment fixtures. The last job, Format, lint, typecheck, and test, needs every lane green; it is the one check in branch protection, so a red lane disables the merge button.

[V shows the security workflows; V again returns.] Beside it, CodeQL, Gitleaks, release security and GitGuardian report into the Security tab without blocking the merge.

title: Deploy scans and signs the exact bundle, then activates only if healthy
say: The merge to dev starts Deploy dev. Its first gate polls the Quality run for this exact merge commit; if that run fails, the deploy refuses and the host is unto
transition: Only then does the runner touch AWS.
script:
The merge to dev starts Deploy dev. It first waits for the Quality run on this exact merge commit; if that fails, the host is untouched. release.py builds one tar with the runtime and web images. scan-release.py extracts those exact images, writes a CycloneDX SBOM and Trivy report for each, and stops on any High or Critical finding before upload. attest-build-provenance then signs the tar and the manifest.

[V shows the second half; V returns.] For upload, GitHub holds no AWS keys: OIDC gives a one-hour role session limited to this repository and dev. The host checks the tar’s SHA-256, starts the candidate and activates it only when health is ready; otherwise it restores the previous release.

title: ZAP scans hosted dev after every deploy: 0 High, 4 Medium (CSP)
say: DAST runs as a second job that needs the deploy. It uses the OWASP ZAP baseline action: a spider and an AJAX spider crawl the single-page app for two minutes, a
transition: That completes the pipeline. Here is everything it checks for, in one table.
script:
After every deploy, a second job runs the OWASP ZAP baseline against the hosted site: a spider and an AJAX spider crawl it for two minutes and passive rules inspect every response, unauthenticated and without attacks, because hosted dev holds shared data. It is report-only.

[V shows the real results; V returns.] This deploy found zero High and four Medium alerts, all from one Content Security Policy gap: our full policy is served Report-Only, so directives such as form-action are effectively unrestricted. The fix is to enforce that policy once its reports are clean.

title: SAST findings are triaged with reasons; SCA blocked merges until fixed
say: SAST is CodeQL with the security-extended query suite on three languages: our TypeScript and JavaScript, the Python deployment scripts, and the workflow files t
transition: Next, dependencies, where a real advisory blocked us.
script:
SAST is CodeQL with the security-extended suite on TypeScript, Python and the workflow files, on every pull request, push and weekly. In pull request 592 it raised three medium alerts, 54 to 56, in the load-test script; we dismissed them as used in tests with a written reason, because that harness never ships in the image.

[V shows SCA; V returns.] SCA is the production dependency audit inside the required check. On 24 October a new advisory marked zod below 4.6.6 as high severity; Quality turned red and two pull requests could not merge until PR 591 added a scoped override. The retained audit now shows zero vulnerabilities across 674 production dependencies.

title: The pipeline caught problems that source-level tests could not
say: Six technical findings. First, on 24 October a new zod advisory turned the audit red with no change from us, and the gate blocked two pull requests until PR 591
transition: Now the live route through GitHub.
script: The technical findings. A new zod advisory blocked merges with no change from us until PR 591 fixed it. Alpine removed the FFmpeg version we pinned, so the image stopped building. An audit of our own pipeline found we scanned a rebuilt image rather than the deployed one; PR 595 moved the gate onto the exact bundle and added the manifest and attestation. Gitleaks reported twenty-seven historical false positives, so we allowlisted exact values. And Cognito code passed its tests while its runtime dependencies were missing from the image. The lesson: verify what ships, not just the source.

title: Load and stress: 100 users pass; the breakpoint is 200, set by the database bridge
say: Load and stress: 100 users pass; the breakpoint is 200, set by the database bridge
script:
Now the quality attributes. Performance was measured with a scripted load test against hosted dev: a Node HTTP runner drives the real API through CloudFront, Node and PostgreSQL, each user waits three to seven seconds between actions, and the mix is ninety-five percent reads. A stage passes with p95 under two seconds and errors under one percent. One to one hundred users all passed: at one hundred, p95 was 1.34 seconds, 17.8 requests per second, zero errors. This morning we pushed further. One hundred and fifty users still passed at 1.66 seconds. The breakpoint is two hundred users: p95 rose to 3.03 seconds, with still zero errors, and throughput saturated at twenty-nine requests per second, eighty percent of linear. At three hundred we stopped the ramp. The system fails by queueing, not by rejecting requests. The limiting factor is not the host CPU, which stayed under twenty-five percent, and not a rate limiter: every database call blocks the single Node event loop on one PostgreSQL client, so every request, even health, waits in the same queue.

[Cite if asked] 1–100 users: 180 s steady stages (26 Oct); 150–300: 60 s stress stages (27 Oct). Every database call waits through Atomics.wait on a single pg client (server/src/postgres/database.ts, sync-worker.ts). Load-generator CPU peaked at 26% of one core, event-loop p99 ≤ 22 ms; zero 429s, 5xx, timeouts or socket errors.

title: The capacity model, checked by the stress test, shows where to scale next
say: Every steady stage passed: 6,038 requests and zero errors.
At one hundred users, p95 was 1.34 seconds and throughput was 17.84 requests per second.
The capacity chart projects one and two API hosts from the quiet-host measurements.
transition: We can take questions using the backup map.
script: Scalability: the capacity model fitted on the one-to-one-hundred run predicted a ceiling of about twenty-two requests per second and a knee near one hundred and sixteen users. The stress test confirms its shape and shows it is about 1.4 times conservative: the measured knee lies between one hundred and fifty and two hundred users, and saturation between twenty-nine and thirty-six requests per second. So the scale-out path follows the bottleneck. First, asynchronous persistence with a bounded connection pool, which removes the serialization. Second, a second API host behind a load balancer, which doubles the modelled ceiling; at two hundred and fifty users the mean drops from 6.4 to 1.1 seconds. Third, a separate media worker keeps film compilation off the API host. A larger instance alone would add little, because the CPU is not saturated. Maintainability is the pipeline we just walked through: those internal changes must pass the same behavioural tests, both database dialects, the exact-image scan and the health-gated deploy. Thank you; I am ready for questions.

title: Keyless AWS access and a health check decide activation

[Detail for C6: press V to return.] GitHub has no AWS keys. The job exchanges its OIDC token for a one-hour role session, and the role trusts only this repository, the dev environment and refs/heads/dev. The runner checks the host is running, opens port 22 for its own address only with a short-lived key, ships the bundle and streams the hosted settings from a private S3 object.

On the host, the uploaded tar must match the built tar’s SHA-256. The installer starts the candidate images and activates them only when health is ready and the running image IDs match; otherwise it restores the previous release and the job turns red. Then the public health endpoint is checked, SSH is closed and the key deleted, and the DAST job starts.

title: DAST: 0 High, 4 Medium, all from one Content Security Policy gap
say: Here are the real ZAP results for the deployed commit: zero High, four Medium, seven Low and six informational alert types. All four Medium alerts are Content S
transition: Tests and coverage complete the catalogue.
script:
[Detail for C8: press V to return.] Here are the real ZAP results for the deployed commit: zero High, four Medium, seven Low and six informational alert types. All four Medium alerts are Content Security Policy findings.

Take the first one. ZAP sent a GET to the hosted home page, robots.txt and sitemap.xml, read the Content-Security-Policy header, and found only frame-ancestors none. Directives such as form-action do not fall back to default-src, so they are effectively unrestricted. The informational alert explains why: our full policy is served as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, so browsers report violations but do not enforce them. The fix is to promote that policy to enforced once its reports are clean. The Low findings are missing hardening headers and the nginx version string.

title: A commit carries tests, inventory and deployment evidence
say: Issue branches reach protected dev through a PR and green Quality.

The artifact is the built image pair, not a new build on the host.
transition: The pipeline shows where each decision happens.
script:
Source management starts with a focused issue branch and a pull request to protected dev. The required Quality result belongs to the exact commit. Once merged, that same source revision triggers dev deployment. The artifact flow matters because a passing test run and a deployed application must be connected by identity.

Quality retains root JUnit, server results and coverage, frontend Jest JSON and coverage, and the production dependency audit report. Deployment retains the runtime and web image inventories, the exact-image Trivy reports, the security manifest and the deployable tarball. Signed provenance binds the retained bundle and manifest to the workflow. After deployment, the ZAP reports describe the running hosted target. The host receives the built image pair in the verified bundle. It does not independently rebuild the application from a moving branch. These artifact families let us move from a source question to a test, package, scan or running-page result without treating those as interchangeable evidence.

title: Pipeline decisions separate merge gates from host activation
say: Read the decision points: scope, Quality, image security and candidate health.
Only aggregate Quality is branch-required; deployment has its own enforcing steps.
ZAP scans hosted dev after successful activation and reports its findings.
transition: Here are the security procedures inside those lanes.
script:
There are several decisions inside this activity view. First, change classification decides whether the commit needs application checks or is documentation-only. A code change fans out across parallel static, client, server, PostgreSQL, root and deployment-fixture lanes. The aggregate fails on a failed or unexpectedly skipped required lane. Production dependency audit is part of that aggregate.

Second, deployment waits for a successful dev Quality run for the same commit. It builds and verifies the bundle, inventories the exact runtime and web images and scans those images. High or Critical findings at that exact-bundle gate stop host upload. This is a deployment gate even though the independent scan workflows are not branch-required checks.

Third, the host installs a candidate and checks it before activation. Failure takes the restoration path. Once the host is serving, the passive ZAP baseline spiders hosted dev and publishes its report. SAST and the other security reports remain visible as their own lanes. The distinction is operational: branch protection requires the aggregate Quality context; a deployment step can independently stop the upload; a reporting lane retains findings for triage. The words BLOCKS and REPORTS in the figure refer to those specific decisions.
label: B27

title: Hosted dev activates after candidate health succeeds
say: OIDC gives the workflow temporary deploy credentials.
The host checks the candidate before switching current.
This run passed its public health check after installation.
transition: The technical findings show why those package and runtime checks matter.
script:
The deployment view puts the logical design onto hosted dev. GitHub Actions obtains temporary deploy credentials through OIDC. It ships the verified bundle to the Lightsail host, where nginx fronts the Node process. The application uses PostgreSQL, private S3 storage, Cognito and web push. CloudFront is the public edge.

Activation is a host decision. The installer prepares a candidate, verifies its health, then switches current. If the candidate is unhealthy, the installer restores the previous current. The deployment run then checks the public health endpoint. In our selected run, install completed at fifteen oh two forty-one UTC and the public check passed. The topology explains the runtime boundary, while the workflow and host installer explain who makes each decision. The following findings are examples of defects that escaped a narrower source-only view.
label: B30

title: Packaging and runtime boundaries exposed useful defects
say: A locked dependency tree can still meet a new advisory, and a pinned package can disappear.
Refactoring must include packaging consumers; realtime must be checked through the service worker.
Whole-interaction tests caught the failed retry path.
transition: Now follow one deployment run from Quality through artifacts and hosted health.
script:
Five findings explain the checks we chose. A new zod advisory turned the production audit red even with a lockfile. The scoped dependency update restored a clean audit. Separately, Alpine removed the pinned FFmpeg package version, so the image failed before vulnerability scanning; the package pin had to move to the available version.

A schema refactor moved the registry while deployment packaging still read the old location. Updating the packaging consumer restored bundle verification. In the PWA, service-worker forwarding prevented SSE cancellation from reaching upstream; repeated group changes then exhausted stream limits. Keeping SSE browser-owned repaired that lifetime. Finally, the failed-capture retry needed a behavioural test of the recovery path. The common lesson is to exercise the real boundary: the package repository, the built image, the service worker, or the full interaction. We can now see how those concerns appear in one retained deployment run.

title: Durable claims keep repeated cycle work safe
say: Polling finds work but does not make repeated execution safe.
We compared polling alone and object hierarchies with persisted state and durable jobs.
Durable claims reject stale completion; MediaStore supplies the storage Strategy role.
transition: The sequence shows where those checks happen.
script: A scheduler tick can repeat, and an old worker can finish after its lease expires. We compared polling alone, State or Command object hierarchies, and persisted state with a durable job. We chose the durable job with lease and generation checks: expensive rendering runs outside the transaction, then finalisation proves that this worker still owns the current claim. Storage creates a second design problem: duplicated backend branches would spread through the worker. Instead we inject the MediaStore Strategy. LocalMediaStore and PrivateS3MediaStore supply the implementations; the S3 transport Adapter translates the SDK operations. The pattern roles are labelled on the real design elements.

Every pipeline page uses the same key. The colour and the first word of a box tell you what happens when it fails. Orange, BLOCKS MERGE: the required Quality check turns red and the pull request cannot merge. Blue, BLOCKS DEPLOY: the deploy stops before upload or before activation, and hosted dev keeps the release it already has. Purple: a platform rule or a human approval, such as push protection or the review on main. Dashed grey, REPORTS: the finding is recorded and visible, but it never stops a merge or a deployment.

Hexagons are decision points. A yes continues the flow; a no stops it. The yellow page shape is a retained artifact, a cylinder is a store, and a box with depth is a running host.

Secrets are checked in three places. At push time, GitHub push protection rejects known provider key patterns before they reach the repository. On the pull request, GitGuardian scans the new commits. The default rules flagged migration identifiers and two test keys as generic API keys. Rather than silence the rule, the allowlist requires the exact file and the exact value, so a real key in the same file would still be found. The current result is zero findings.

title: Trivy blocks risky images; IaC risks need dated exceptions
say: Trivy scans our two container images twice. Release security scans candidate images on pull requests and pushes. The deployment then scans the images inside the
transition: The image scan feeds the SBOM and provenance.
script:
Trivy scans our two container images twice. Release security scans candidate images on pull requests and pushes. The deployment then scans the images inside the exact bundle it will upload, and that second scan is the one that blocks: any High or Critical stops the upload. For this deployment both images had zero High and Critical. The runtime image has one Medium in zlib with a fix available, and two Unknown entries in musl.

For infrastructure as code, Trivy config scans Terraform and Dockerfiles. It found fifteen issues: seven Low and eight High. Every High must match exactly one exception with an owner, a reason and an expiry date. Most are about customer-managed KMS keys and a WAF that would add cost. The exceptions expire on 31 October, and after that the job fails until each risk is reviewed again.

script: The server suite has one thousand and six tests. Each starts the real HTTP server and calls real routes. This privacy test signs in as a member of another group and expects a 403 with no content for every protected resource.
label: T3

title: The server suite runs again on PostgreSQL 17
say: The same suite passes 989 tests on PostgreSQL 17.
transition: Repository rules guard the architecture itself.
script: The same suite runs again on PostgreSQL seventeen in a throwaway container: nine hundred and eighty-nine pass. That catches SQL that works on SQLite but not on the hosted database.
label: T4

title: Repository tests stop the architecture and policies drifting
say: Architecture, PWA, classifier and Terraform policies are tested like code.
transition: Deployment scripts get the same treatment.
script: Repository tests check our own rules. The architecture guard is itself tested: we plant a bad import in each layer and expect two violations. Terraform and deploy policy, such as only deploying a commit that passed Quality, are tested the same way.
label: T5

title: Deployment scripts are tested offline with injected failures
say: Eleven cloud-free fixtures inject deployment failures.
transition: Now the browser tests.
script: Deployment scripts are tested offline. Eleven fixtures replace tar, chown and the health check with fakes, then inject failures. A failed restore must leave the previous state intact.
label: T6

title: Playwright drives the exported app in a real browser
say: 41 browser tests join for main; one real-account journey runs on demand.
transition: The exported PWA is checked as installed.
script: Playwright drives the exported web app in Chromium at iPhone sizes: forty-one tests, required for pull requests to main. A longer Firefox journey uses real accounts: owner, invited member and outsider, through to the next cycle.
label: T7

title: The PWA build is checked the way it will be installed
say: The exported PWA build, offline shell and cache rules are tested.
transition: Accessibility uses the same browser run.
script: The exported PWA is tested as it will be installed: manifest, service worker, offline page and icons. A service-worker rule test makes sure private media and API answers never enter the cache.
label: T8

title: Axe and keyboard tests check the main screens for WCAG 2.1 AA
say: Axe scans and keyboard tests fail on serious or critical violations.
transition: Security is tested at two levels.
script: Accessibility runs in the same browser job. Axe scans the main screens against WCAG 2.1 A and AA, and two keyboard tests check focus. Serious or critical violations fail the build.
label: T9

title: A scripted load test drives the hosted API in five stages
say: Five stages from 1 to 100 users; pass rule p95 under 2 seconds and under 1% errors.
transition: Here are the results.
script: Performance has its own test. A Node runner drives the hosted API through CloudFront in five stages, from one to one hundred concurrent users. Each user acts, then waits three to seven seconds. The mix is ninety-five percent reads. Every stage must keep p95 under two seconds and errors under one percent.
label: T11

title: 100 concurrent users stay under the 2-second target, error-free
say: All five stages pass: 6,038 requests, zero errors, p95 1.34 s at 100 users.
transition: Now the pipeline that runs these tests.
script: All five stages passed: six thousand and thirty-eight requests, zero errors. At one hundred users p95 was one point three four seconds, with seventeen point eight requests per second. I return to capacity in the system demo. Now, the pipeline that runs all of these tests.
label: T12

Sunday 19:00 in the group time zone; snooze seven days.

One film combines the group’s accepted inputs.
720 × 1280 · 30 fps · normalised audio.

script:

The film is now available to the group. Open the premiere and watch the contributions together. The player exposes moment segments and lets the viewer move between them. The output is a portrait film at seven-twenty by twelve-eighty, thirty frames per second, with normalised audio. Press M only if you want the film sound. Pause at the end screen. The film connects the sealed contribution habit to the shared payoff we described at the start.
label: F10
